newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt vows end to crisis, Yeltsin to move.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt vows end to crisis, Yeltsin to move.

text.p: The Russian government, seeking a political consensus as Boris Yeltsin readies his comeback from illness, agreed a broad economic plan on Thursday to transform crisis into growth during the president's four-year term.

"This is the fundamental, basic, main document around which our whole economic universe will spin," Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told the cabinet. But details of how to achieve the planned economic growth have yet to be worked out.
"It should be a direct continuation and realisation of the ideas and policies of President Boris Yeltsin's four-year election campaign programme," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying.

Chernomyrdin later chaired the first meeting of a new cross-party Consultative Council set up by Yeltsin to draw communists and other opposition groups into policy-making. The leader of the communists stayed away.

The president's press service said Yeltsin would leave the Central Clinical Hospital on Friday for the Barvikha government sanatorium outside Moscow, two and a half weeks after undergoing a quintuple heart bypass operation.
Yeltsin, who said in his first television appearance on Wednesday that he felt fighting fit, could be back at work in the Kremlin by the end of the year, a spokesman said.
But the head of his medical staff warned Yeltsin risked overdoing things by appearing on television.
"Filming is a serious burden, even for a healthy person, and all the more so for a patient who had a heart operation on November 5," Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov said.

The depth of the economic crisis Yeltsin will face on his return was underlined by news of an alarming fuel shortage in the Pacific city of Vladivostok and word of "difficult" talks with the International Monetary Fund on releasing loan monies.

Chernomyrdin, prime minister for four years, appeared to admit weaknesses in policy which have left millions in deep poverty and prompted more than 40 percent of voters to back Yeltsin's communist opponent in July's presidential election.
The medium-term policy from 1997 to 2000, could be more significant than the dramatic free market reforms of the past four years, Chernomyrdin was quoted as telling the cabinet.
"This is the transition to real economic growth, not just words, and real structural rebuilding, not just on paper."
The prime minister said the aim of the programme was "economic growth through social accord and consolidation".

Investment, new technology, financial stability, a reliable social welfare system, free markets and law and order were all necessary elements in that, he said. Ministries must now come up with concrete policies on how to ensure these exist.

Concerned by communist strength in parliament, the Kremlin is keen to draw its opponents into endorsing key policies, like those on the broad lines of economic reform. Yeltsin promised to do more to ease social problems during the election campaign.

However, his election opponent, communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, did not attend the first meeting of the Consultative Council -- in protest, he said, at the presence of Anatoly Chubais, the Kremlin chief-of-staff who stood in for Yeltsin.

Communists were represented by Gennady Seleznyov, speaker of the State Duma lower house. Seleznyov had dropped his objections to sitting down with Chubais, whom the opposition accuses of usurping power in Yeltsin's absence.

The council discussed the peace process in breakaway Chechnya and the political crisis in Belarus, where Moscow's attempts to mediate between President Alexander Lukashenko and the Minsk parliament have produced little result.
There were signs, however, that the opposition is not about to give the convalescing president an easy ride.

A leading communist legislator was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying the Duma would debate on Friday newspaper allegations that Chubais and other Yeltsin aides had been involved in illegal financing of the president's campaign.
